To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the methylation levels were significantly increased at differentially methylations regions (DMRs)-of the gene, in fetuses of gestational diabetes (P = 1.5E-05).

the methylation levels of 3 CpG sites of DMRs of the GNAS gene in the umbilical cord lymphocytes from infants born to gestationally diabetic mothers were significantly higher than in the infants born to non-diabetic mothers.
the methylation levels of 3 CpG sites of the GNAS DMR were significantly higher in the infants of mothers with GDM compared to the infants of mothers without GDM.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epigenetic mechanisms underlying the increased risk of metabolic syndrome in offspring of GDM.
the relationship between maternal diabetes during pregnancy and epigenetic changes in the fetus.

the epigenetic changes in the offspring of gestational diabetes mellitus and the possible mechanisms linking intrauterine exposure of gestational diabetes with increased risk of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease in the offspring.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GNAS DMR methylation may be among the possible mechanisms associating maternal diabetes with increased risk of health problems of offspring in later life.
maternal GDM-induced epigenetic changes at GNAS DMP may be among the potential mechanisms linking maternal GDN with high risk of health issues in later life of the offspring.
maternal GDM induces epigenetic alterations in the GNAS DMR, which may contribute to the high risk of metabolic disease in later life of their offspring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
maternal GDM-induced epigenetic alterations in fetal genome may play an important role in the high risk for metabolic disease in offspring.
the hypermethylation of GNAS in GDM offspring is associated with increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and obesity in later life.
maternal GDM induced hypermethylation at site 4, 6 and 7 of the GNAS DMR which might play a role in the association between GDM and increased metabolic diseases in the offspring.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GNAS DMR hypermethylation may be a potential epigenetic marker of GDM.
GDM-induced epigenetic alterations may be a potential mechanism linking maternal GDM and metabolic diseases in later offspring life.

the methylation levels in differentially methylated genes in GDM offspring were significantly different from those in normal pregnancy, and the methylation levels of some sites in GNAS DMR were significantly associated with maternal GDM.
